gloss: take captive, carry off; captivity, captives
summary: To take people captive in war and lead them away, or to carry off cattle and goods: the act of the raider and the conqueror, from the Amalekites at Ziklag to Babylon, and the curse that ends in exile (Deu 28:41). Its nouns name captivity itself (“into captivity”, with the sword and the plunder), the captives as a body, and “the captivity”, the exiles who came back with Ezra and Nehemiah; in the phrase “turn back the captivity” Yahweh brings his people home and restores what they lost. Psalm 68 has God “lead captivity captive”, which Eph 4:8 applies to the risen Christ, and Isa 61:1 sends the anointed one to proclaim release to captives (Luk 4:18). Arabic sabā, Jewish Aramaic שְׁבָא, Ugaritic šby and the Peshitta’s ܫܒܐ share the sense.

words.gloss: take captive, carry off; (niphal) be taken captive
words.summary: About forty-five times in the qal and eight in the niphal. Its object is people taken in war or raid and led away alive, or cattle and goods driven off; it goes with בָּזַז “plunder” and is undone when the captor lets the captives go. The active participle שֹׁבֶה is the captor. Five qal tokens the database files under שׁוּב (Gen 34:29; 1Ki 8:48; Jer 41:14; 2Ch 6:38; 25:12) belong here and are cited here.

senses.definition: Seize people in war or a raid and lead them away alive, not killing them: women, children and men taken to the captor’s land.

evidence.note: The Amalekites “took captive the women … they killed no one, but carried them off and went their way”: taking captive is leading away alive.
“All their little ones and their wives they took captive and plundered”: the people taken, the goods plundered (בָּזַז).
Israel took captive the women of Midian and their little ones.
The king of Arad fought Israel “and took some of them captive”.
“And you take its captives captive (וְשָׁבִיתָ שִׁבְיוֹ)”: the law of the captive woman follows.
Raiders of Aram took captive a young girl from the land of Israel, who served Naaman’s wife.
Ishmael took captive the remnant at Mizpah, the king’s daughters among them, and set out for Ammon.
Israel took captive 200,000 women, sons and daughters of Judah, and plundered much spoil.
The prophet Oded: “send back the captives you have taken captive from your brothers”.
“Until Asshur takes you captive.”
Solomon’s prayer: “and their captors take them captive to the land of the enemy, far or near”.
They pray toward the land, the city and the house “in the land of their enemies who took them captive”.
Laban: “you have carried away my daughters like captives of the sword (כִּשְׁבֻיוֹת חָרֶב)”, the passive participle.
“To proclaim release (דְּרוֹר) to captives (לִשְׁבוּיִם)”, the passive participle: those held captive, set over against liberty.
Jesus reads Isa 61:1 in the synagogue at Nazareth and says it is fulfilled that day (Luk 4:21); the Peshitta has ܠܫܒܝܐ, “to the captives”.
Nebuchadnezzar will burn the houses of Egypt’s gods “and take them captive”: the idols carried off with their people.
“You ascended on high, you led captivity captive (שָׁבִיתָ שֶּׁבִי), you received gifts among men”: the victor leads his captives in his train.
Paul quotes Psa 68:19 of Christ ascended: “he led captivity captive and gave gifts to men”; the Peshitta has ܘܫܒܐ ܫܒܝܬܐ.
“Arise, Barak, and lead your captives captive (וּשֲׁבֵה שֶׁבְיְךָ)”: the same phrase in Deborah’s song.

senses.definition: Drive off livestock or take away property as booty, the same act done to possessions.

evidence.note: “They took captive their livestock: fifty thousand camels, two hundred and fifty thousand sheep, two thousand donkeys, and a hundred thousand people.”
Asa’s men “carried off sheep in abundance and camels”.
The Philistines and Arabs carried off all the property in the king’s house, and his sons and wives.
“In the day that strangers carried off his wealth”: Edom stood aloof when Jerusalem was taken.

senses.definition: The one who has taken people captive and holds them.

evidence.note: “All their captors held them fast; they refused to let them go”: the captor keeps hold, the opposite of letting go (שִׁלַּח).
Israel “will take captive their captors (שֹׁבִים לְשֹׁבֵיהֶם) and rule over their oppressors”.
By the rivers of Babylon “our captors asked us for a song”.
Yahweh “gave them compassion before all their captors”.
Hezekiah: if you return to Yahweh, your brothers and sons will find compassion before their captors and return to this land.

senses.gloss: be taken captive, be carried off
senses.definition: Be seized and led away by an enemy; of an animal, be driven off by raiders.

evidence.note: Abram heard “that his brother had been taken captive” and pursued the kings to Dan.
At Ziklag “their wives and their sons and their daughters had been taken captive”.
“In the land where they have been taken captive”.
“Because Yahweh’s flock has been taken captive.”
“Among the nations where they have been carried captive” the survivors will remember Yahweh.
An animal left in keeping that “dies, or is hurt, or is driven off (נִשְׁבָּה)” with no one seeing.

evidence.locator: αἰχμαλωτεύω renders שָׁבָה ×5, with inflected forms ᾐχμαλώτευσαν ×4 and ᾐχμαλώτευσας ×2 counted apart

evidence.note: “He led captive (ᾐχμαλώτευσεν) captivity”, quoting Psa 68:19.
“They will be led captive into all the nations.”
“Taking me captive to the law of sin.”
“Taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ.”

parallels.note: “Plunder”: the people are taken captive, the goods plundered.

opposites.note: “Let go, send away”: captors hold fast and will not let go.

words.summary: Fifty times: the state of captivity that people go into, and the captives themselves taken as a body or one by one. With the article in Ezra and Nehemiah, “the captivity” is the company of exiles who returned. The feminine שְׁבִיָּה “captive woman” (Isa 52:2) is counted with it.

senses.definition: Being carried off by an enemy to his land: one of the judgments of war beside the sword, death, famine and plunder.

evidence.note: “Those for death, to death; those for the sword, to the sword; those for famine, to famine; and those for captivity, to captivity.”
“If anyone leads into captivity, into captivity he goes”, in the words of Jer 15:2 and 43:11; the Peshitta has ܫܒܝܐ.
The curse: “you shall father sons and daughters, but they shall not be yours, for they shall go into captivity”.
“Her children have gone into captivity before the adversary.”
Pashhur and his house will go into captivity to Babylon and die there.
“All your adversaries, every one of them, shall go into captivity.”
Bel and Nebo cannot save the burden; “they themselves have gone into captivity”.
Yahweh “gave his strength into captivity, his splendour into the enemy’s hand”: the ark taken at Aphek.
“They shall stumble by sword and flame, by captivity and plunder.”
“Given into the hand of the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, to plunder and to shame of face.”
No-Amon “went into exile, into captivity”.

senses.definition: With the article, the people who had been carried to Babylon and came back to the land, as a body.

evidence.note: “The sons of the province who came up out of the captivity of the exile, whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away to Babylon, and returned to Jerusalem and Judah.”
“All who had come from the captivity to Jerusalem” began the house of God.
“The Jews who had escaped, who were left from the captivity.”
“All the assembly who had returned from the captivity made booths.”

senses.definition: Those who have been taken, as a body or one person: the captive in the dungeon, the captives brought to the camp.

evidence.note: “They brought the captives (הַשְּׁבִי), the spoil and the plunder to Moses.”
“From the firstborn of Pharaoh on his throne to the firstborn of the captive in the dungeon”: the lowest of the land.
“Can the prey be taken from the mighty, or the captives of the righteous be delivered?”
Yahweh answers that even the captives of the mighty will be taken back.
The Chaldean “gathers captives like sand”.
“Loose the bonds of your neck, captive daughter of Zion (שְׁבִיָּה)”, the feminine.
He will carry their gods, their images and their precious vessels into Egypt “in captivity”.

evidence.locator: Psa.68.19, שֶּׁבִי → αἰχμαλωσίαν; Jer.15.2, שְּׁבִי → αἰχμαλωσίαν; αἰχμαλωσία renders שְׁבִי ×27

evidence.note: “He led captive captivity (αἰχμαλωσίαν).”
“If anyone gathers into captivity (αἰχμαλωσίαν), into captivity he goes.”

evidence.locator: Isa.61.1, שְׁבוּיִם → αἰχμαλώτοις; Isa.52.2, שְׁבִיָּה → αἰχμάλωτος

evidence.note: “To proclaim release to captives (αἰχμαλώτοις)”, quoting Isa 61:1.

parallels.note: “Sword”: captivity is one of the judgments beside the sword.

words.gloss: captivity; (with שׁוּב) the captivity turned back, fortunes restored
words.summary: Written שְׁבִית and שְׁבוּת, the two often as written and read text of the same word. Once plainly “captivity” (Num 21:29); otherwise always the object of שׁוּב in the phrase “turn back the captivity”, where Yahweh gathers his scattered people from the nations into their land (Deu 30:3; Jer 29:14; Ezk 39:25–28). The phrase is used too of Sodom, Moab, Ammon, Elam and Egypt, and of Job, who had not been exiled: Yahweh restores what was lost. The Peshitta’s ܫܒܝܬܐ, the same form, is “captivity” in Eph 4:8, which supports reading the word from this root rather than as a “turning” from שׁוּב.

senses.definition: The state of being taken captive.

evidence.note: Chemosh “has given his sons as fugitives and his daughters into captivity (בַּשְּׁבִית) to Sihon”.

senses.definition: With שׁוּב, Yahweh turns back his people’s captivity: he gathers the exiles from the nations, brings them into the land, and has compassion on them.

evidence.note: “Yahweh your God will turn back your captivity and have compassion on you, and will gather you again from all the peoples where he scattered you”, and bring you into the land your fathers possessed (Deu 30:5).
“I will turn back your captivity and gather you from all the nations … and bring you back to the place from which I sent you into exile.”
“Now I will turn back the captivity of Jacob”; explained in Ezk 39:28, “I sent them into exile among the nations and gathered them into their own land”.
“I will turn back the captivity of my people Israel and Judah … and bring them back to the land I gave their fathers, and they shall possess it.”
“I will turn back the captivity of Judah and of Israel and build them as at the first.”
“I will turn back the captivity of my people Israel; they shall rebuild the ruined cities … and I will plant them on their land, and they shall never again be uprooted” (Amo 9:15).
“At that time I will bring you in … when I turn back your captivity before your eyes.”
“When I turn back the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem, I will gather all the nations” to the valley of Jehoshaphat.
“When Yahweh turns back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice.”
“Turn back our captivity, Yahweh, like streams in the Negev”, after Psa 126:1 has the same phrase with שִׁיבָה of שׁוּב.

senses.gloss: restore the fortunes (of the nations, of Job)
senses.definition: The same phrase of peoples and of a man who were not, or not only, exiles: Yahweh reverses their ruin and restores what they lost.

evidence.note: “Yahweh turned back the captivity of Job when he prayed for his friends, and gave Job twice as much as he had before”: Job had lost goods, children and health, not his land.
“I will turn back their captivity, the captivity of Sodom and her daughters and of Samaria and her daughters”: Sodom was overthrown, not exiled.
“I will turn back the captivity of Egypt and bring them back to the land of Pathros.”
Moab.
The sons of Ammon.
Elam.

evidence.locator: Ezk.39.25, שְׁבוּת → αἰχμαλωσίαν; Amo.9.14, שְׁבוּת → αἰχμαλωσίαν; Psa.126.4, שְׁבִית → αἰχμαλωσίαν; Num.21.29, שְּׁבִית → αἰχμάλωτοι

phrases.gloss: turn back the captivity; restore the fortunes

words.summary: Fourteen times: the captives taken together, as in the story of Oded in 2 Chronicles 28, and the captivity they are in.

senses.gloss: the captives, a body of captives
senses.definition: All the people taken captive, spoken of as one company.

evidence.note: “Send back the captives (הַשִּׁבְיָה) you have taken captive from your brothers.”
“The armed men left the captives and the plunder before the princes.”
The captives were clothed, fed, anointed and brought to Jericho.
Aram “carried away a great number of captives to Damascus”.
“And you see among the captives a woman of beautiful form.”
“With the blood of the slain and of the captives.”

senses.definition: The state of being a captive, and the land where captives are held.

evidence.note: “She shall put off the clothes of her captivity.”
“Your sons are taken into captivity (בַּשֶּׁבִי) and your daughters into captivity (בַּשִּׁבְיָה)”: the two nouns in parallel.
“Give them up to be plundered in a land of captivity.”
“In the land of their captivity.”
“I will save your seed from the land of their captivity, and Jacob shall return.”

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܫܒܐ (šḇā), for αἰχμαλωτίζω and αἰχμαλωτεύω: captives of war, and in Paul the captivity of a man to the law of sin and of thoughts to Christ.

senses.definition: Lead someone away as a captive; of sin or an unclean spirit, hold a man in its power.

evidence.note: ܘܫܒܐ ܫܒܝܬܐ, “and he led captivity captive”, quoting Psa 68:19.
“Another law in my members … takes me captive (ܘܫܒܐ ܠܝ) to the law of sin.”
“We take captive (ܘܫܒܝܢܢ) every thought to the obedience of Christ.”
Those who creep into houses “and take captive (ܘܫܒܝܢ) weak women”.
The unclean spirit had held the man captive (ܕܫܒܐ) many times; the Greek has συνηρπάκει, “seized”.

senses.definition: Be carried away captive by an enemy.

evidence.note: “They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive (ܘܢܫܬܒܘܢ) to every nation, and Jerusalem will be trodden down by the nations.”

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܫܒܝܐ (šḇāyā), “captive”, for αἰχμάλωτος in Luk 4:18 and for Paul’s fellow prisoners (συναιχμάλωτος).

senses.definition: One held captive; with “of mine”, a fellow prisoner.

evidence.note: “To proclaim release to the captives (ܠܫܒܝܐ)”, Isa 61:1.
Aristarchus, Paul’s fellow captive.
Epaphras, “my fellow captive in Christ Jesus”.
Andronicus and Junia, “my fellow captives”.

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܫܒܝܐ (šeḇyā), “captivity”, the Hebrew שְׁבִי.

senses.definition: Being led away captive, as a judgment.

evidence.note: “If anyone leads into captivity (ܒܫܒܝܐ), into captivity he goes”, as Jer 15:2.

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܫܒܝܬܐ (šḇītā), the same form as Hebrew שְׁבִית.

senses.definition: The captives taken as a body, led in the victor’s train.

evidence.note: ܘܫܒܐ ܫܒܝܬܐ, “and he led captivity captive”, for αἰχμαλωσίαν.

cognates.note: Arabic s answers Hebrew ש where the older sound is š. The verbal noun سَبْىٌ is both the taking and the captives, as Hebrew שְׁבִי is both captivity and captives.

cognates.gloss: take captive; lead off, plunder; lead into exile
cognates.note: The meaning matches closely, including leading people into exile, but Ge’ez ṣ́ for Hebrew ש is not the regular correspondence, so the tie is argued, not shown.

evidence.locator: Ge'ez ፄወወ (ṣ́ewäwä), verb: to capture, take captive; to lead off, plunder, loot (as cattle, goods); to lead people into exile; to conquer, subdue

doctrine.statement: Captivity was the curse the law foretold for Israel’s unfaithfulness (Deu 28:41), and “turning back the captivity” is Yahweh gathering them out of all the nations into the land he gave their fathers (Deu 30:3–5; Jer 29:14; Jer 30:3; Ezk 39:25–28). Amos adds that, once planted on their land, they “shall never again be uprooted” (Amo 9:14–15). The return under Ezra and Nehemiah was followed by a new uprooting, which Jesus foretold (Luk 21:24), so that promise still waits: the land promise to Abraham’s seed is literal and its full keeping is future, when the kingdom is restored to Israel (Act 1:6; Act 3:21).

Jesus used the prophets’ pair of judgments, sword and captivity (Jer 15:2), of Jerusalem: when it is surrounded by armies its desolation is near, and its people “will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive into all the nations, and Jerusalem will be trodden down by the nations until the times of the nations are fulfilled” (Luk 21:20–24). This was fulfilled when Rome took Jerusalem in AD 70 and carried its people away, and the treading down lasts until the times of the nations end.

Psa 68:19 pictures God going up on high as victor, leading his captives and receiving gifts among men. Paul applies it to Christ: he who descended to the lower parts of the earth ascended far above all, and gave gifts: apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers (Eph 4:8–11). Peter says the same of the man God raised: exalted to God’s right hand, he received from the Father the promised holy spirit and poured it out (Act 2:32–33). The gifts are God’s power given through the risen Son.

Isa 61:1 sends the one anointed with Yahweh’s spirit to proclaim release to captives, and Jesus read it at Nazareth and said, “Today this scripture is fulfilled in your hearing” (Luk 4:18–21). Paul names the captivity: the law of sin in his members takes him captive (Rom 7:23), and the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus sets him free from the law of sin and death (Rom 8:2).

note: Drafted 2026-11-19. BDB's v.ao.ab (שְׁבִי n.m.) and v.ao.ac (שָׁבִי adj. “captive”) count the same fifty tokens, so only v.ao.ab is named; שְׁבִיָּה (Isa 52:2) is cited under שְׁבִי. שְׁבִית/שְׁבוּת is entered here: shuv.json (שׁוּב) left it out and asked whether it belongs there; Num 21:29 (plain “captivity”, no שׁוּב), the exile-and-gathering verses, and the Peshitta’s ܫܒܝܬܐ for αἰχμαλωσία in Eph 4:8 favour this root, while Job 42:10 and Ezk 16:53 show the phrase widened to “restore”; shuv.json’s own sense of the phrase under שׁוּב is left there. The five qal tokens shuv.json says the database files under שׁוּב (Gen 34:29; 1Ki 8:48; Jer 41:14; 2Ch 6:38; 25:12) are cited here. Left out: שְׁבוֹ “agate” (v.ao.af, Exo 28:19; 39:12), a loan from Akkadian šubû (Oracc cmawro/x000021550, a semiprecious stone), which should be its own entry; תִּשְׁבֶּה/תִּשְׁבִּי Tishbe, the Tishbite (v.ao.aj, v.ao.ak), a place and its gentilic, not a personal name, and v.ao.aj’s tokens are really תּוֹשָׁב of ישׁב (yashav.json); the names שְׁבוּאֵל/שׁוּבָאֵל Shebuel/Shubael (v.ao.ai; the Shubael spelling points to שׁוּב), שֹׁבַי Shobai (v.ao.ah) and שֹׁבִי Shobi (v.ao.ag, an Ammonite), whose tie to “take captive” is not clear (a participle “captor” is possible), so no name files were written. Brief’s שְׁבִי tokens Gen 38:11 etc. are imperatives of ישׁב. Not consulted: DULAT for Ugaritic šby and its texts (only the Proto-Semitic list), Krahmalkov for Punic šb, Dillmann and Leslau for Ge’ez ṣ́ewäwä (Wiktionary only), CAL; a Sabaean sbʾ “wage war” (with s1, not the same sibilant) is a lead not followed; an Akkadian verb šabû “take captive” claimed in one lexicon was not found in Oracc. SEDRA: root 1803 ܫܒܐ, lexemes 3098 ܫܒܐ (verb), 3546 ܫܒܝܐ “captive”, 3099 ܫܒܝܐ “captivity”, 3100 ܫܒܝܬܐ “captivity”; Peshitta verses from the database’s Peshitta word list. Open questions: (1) whether שְׁבוּת in שׁוּב שְׁבוּת should be split off to שׁוּב as “a turning” after all; (2) whether Shobai/Shobi (and Shebuel) should get name files under this root.
